cards.front: What is the single biggest advantage of AC over DC?
cards.back: AC can be transformed (stepped up or down with a transformer); DC can't (without electronics).

cards.front: Why transmit power at high voltage?
cards.back: For the same power, higher voltage means less current. Line loss is I²R, so 1/10 the current gives 1/100 the loss, and smaller wire.

cards.front: Is "DC can't be transformed" still strictly true?
cards.back: Not today. Power electronics convert DC to DC (chargers, solar optimizers, HVDC lines). Give the book's answer on the book's test.

cards.front: History check: which event is usually credited with settling AC vs DC lighting?
cards.back: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago (Westinghouse won). The book says 1904 St. Louis.
cards.note: Use the book's answer on the book's test

cards.front: How does AC differ from DC?
cards.back: AC reverses its direction of flow at regular intervals; DC flows one way.

cards.front: Name the three AC waveforms shown.
cards.back: Square, triangle, and sine.

cards.front: How are square waves usually produced?
cards.back: By electronic switching circuits called oscillators.

cards.front: What is a linear wave?
cards.back: One whose voltage changes at a constant rate, so it plots as straight lines (e.g., the triangle wave).
cards.note: 100 V at 2 ms → 50 V at 1 ms

cards.front: Why is the sine wave the most common AC waveform?
cards.back: Every rotating machine (generator or alternator) produces one.

cards.front: How many electrical degrees are in one sine wave?
cards.back: 360°

cards.front: Where does a sine wave hit +peak, zero, and −peak?
cards.back: +peak at 90°, zero at 180°, −peak at 270°, back to zero at 360°.

cards.front: What is a cycle?
cards.back: One complete waveform: 0 → +peak → 0 → −peak → 0 (360°).

cards.front: What is frequency, and what is its unit?
cards.back: The number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
cards.note: 60 Hz in US/Canada; 50 Hz most of the world

cards.front: Formulas linking period and frequency?
cards.back: T = 1/f and f = 1/T (T in seconds, f in Hz).

cards.front: Period of 60 Hz?
cards.back: 1/60 = 16.67 ms; a peak every 8.33 ms.

cards.front: 1200 Hz: time for one cycle?
A cycle takes 0.04 ms. Frequency?
Prefix values: ms, µs, kHz, MHz?
cards.back: ms = 10⁻³ s, µs = 10⁻⁶ s, kHz = 10³ Hz, MHz = 10⁶ Hz

cards.front: Electrical vs mechanical degrees on a 4-pole machine?
cards.back: One mechanical revolution = 720 electrical degrees (2 cycles). They're only equal on a 2-pole machine.

cards.front: What happens to a 60 Hz motor run on 50 Hz?
cards.back: It runs at about 5/6 speed and can overheat. Always check the nameplate frequency.

cards.front: Why does generator voltage follow a sine curve?
cards.back: The loop cuts flux slowly near 0° (moving almost parallel) and fastest at 90° (moving straight across). The cutting rate follows sin θ.
cards.note: 1 V is induced when flux is cut at 1 Wb/s; 1 Wb = 10⁸ lines

cards.front: Instantaneous value formula?
cards.back: e(inst) = E(max) × sin θ
cards.note: Rearranged: E(max) = e/sin θ; sin θ = e/E(max)

cards.front: 100 V peak: voltage at 30°? at 45°?
cards.back: 30°: 100 × 0.5 = 50 V. 45°: 100 × 0.707 = 70.7 V.

cards.front: 138 V peak: voltage at 78°?
246 V at 53°. What's the peak?
350 V peak. At what angle is it 53 V?
cards.back: sin⁻¹(53/350) = 8.7°, and also 180° − 8.7° = 171.3°.
cards.note: Example 15–5. The book gives 8.685° because it rounded early

cards.front: Why does every voltage value occur twice per half-cycle?
cards.back: The wave passes it once rising and once falling: at θ and at 180° − θ. sin⁻¹ only gives the first.

cards.front: What sign is the voltage between 180° and 360°?
cards.back: Negative (sine is negative there). sin 225° = −0.707.

cards.front: How do you handle an angle over 360°?
cards.back: Subtract 360°: 400° is the same as 40°.

cards.front: Angle and time are linked how?
Name the four values used to describe a sine wave.
cards.back: Peak-to-peak, peak, RMS, and average.

cards.front: What is peak (amplitude)?
cards.back: From zero to the highest point in either direction.

cards.front: What is peak-to-peak?
cards.back: From +peak to −peak (2 × peak). It's the easiest value to read off an oscilloscope.

cards.front: 100 V peak AC and 100 V DC each across 100 Ω. Same heat?
cards.back: No. DC: 100 W. AC at 100 V peak: only 50 W, because it's below 100 V most of the time.

cards.front: What does RMS (effective value) mean?
cards.back: The AC value that produces the same heat as that much DC.
cards.note: Root-Mean-Square: square every value, average them, take the root

cards.front: RMS ↔ peak conversions (sine wave)?
354 V peak → RMS?
120 V RMS → peak? peak-to-peak?
Peak values of 208, 240, 277, 480 V systems?
cards.back: 294, 339, 392, 679 V

cards.front: What value do AC voltmeters/ammeters, nameplates and the NEC use?
cards.back: RMS, unless stated otherwise.

cards.front: What value are component voltage ratings (diodes, capacitors, MOVs, ballast maximums) often given in?
cards.back: Peak. Convert the system's RMS voltage to peak before comparing.
cards.note: Practical App 2: 277 V RMS ≈ 392 V peak

cards.front: Do 0.707 and 1.414 work for every waveform?
cards.back: No, only sine waves. Square wave: RMS = peak. Triangle: RMS = 0.577 × peak.

cards.front: Why use a True RMS meter?
cards.back: Average-responding meters assume a sine wave. On distorted loads (VFDs, LED drivers, computers) they can read 20–40% off, usually low.

cards.front: Book typo: "100 V RMS applied to a 100-V resistor" — fix it.
cards.back: It should say a 100-Ω resistor.

cards.front: "It's only 120 V." What does the insulation actually see?
cards.back: About 170 V peak, twice every cycle.

cards.front: What is the average of a full, unrectified sine wave over one cycle?
cards.back: Zero. The + and − halves cancel.
cards.note: Average values only mean something after rectification

cards.front: What does a rectifier do?
cards.back: Uses diodes to let current flow in one direction only, turning AC into DC.

cards.front: Full-wave vs half-wave rectifier?
cards.back: Full-wave (bridge, 4 diodes): both halves flipped positive. Half-wave (1 diode): the negative half is blocked.

cards.front: What are pulsating DC and ripple?
cards.back: Pulsating DC rises and falls but never reverses. Ripple is the bumps in it.

cards.front: Full-wave average formulas?
cards.back: avg = peak × 0.637 = RMS × 0.9

cards.front: Half-wave average formulas?
cards.back: avg = peak × 0.318 = RMS × 0.45 (half of full-wave)

cards.front: 120 V RMS into a full-wave rectifier: average DC?
277 V into a half-wave rectifier: average DC?
88 V peak-to-peak: average value?
cards.back: Halve first: 44 V peak. Then 44 × 0.637 ≈ 28 V.
cards.note: Review Q9: using p-p directly is the classic mistake

cards.front: A capacitor is added after the rectifier. What does the DC read now?
cards.back: Close to peak (≈ 1.414 × RMS), not 0.9 × RMS.
cards.note: 480 V VFD DC bus ≈ 650–680 VDC. Treat it as live until verified discharged.

cards.front: What does a DC voltmeter read on pulsating DC?
cards.back: The average value.

cards.front: What is wavelength (λ)?
cards.back: The distance a radiated wave travels during one cycle.

cards.front: Wavelength formula?
cards.back: λ = 300,000,000 m/s ÷ f (answer in meters)

cards.front: Wavelength at 100 MHz? At 60 Hz?
cards.back: 100 MHz: 3 m. 60 Hz: about 5,000 km (≈3,100 mi), which is why power wiring isn't an antenna.

cards.front: Two characteristics of a resistive load?
cards.back:
1. It produces heat.
2. Voltage and current are in phase.

cards.front: Examples of resistive loads?
cards.back: Heaters, water-heater and range elements, incandescent lamps.

cards.front: In a pure resistive AC circuit, do the DC Ohm's law and power formulas work?
cards.back: Yes, unchanged, as long as every value is RMS.

cards.front: Exception: is an incandescent lamp a constant resistance?
cards.back: No. The cold filament is about 1/10 of its hot resistance, so there's a large inrush at switch-on.

cards.front: Name the three basic types of AC loads.
cards.back: Resistive, inductive, capacitive.

cards.front: Why is power always positive in a resistive AC circuit?
cards.back: Voltage and current always have the same sign: + × + = +, and − × − = +.

cards.front: At what frequency does power pulse in a 60 Hz resistive circuit?
cards.back: 120 Hz (twice line frequency), because it peaks on both half-cycles.

cards.front: Average power vs peak power (resistive)?
cards.back: Average = ½ of peak. W = E(RMS) × I(RMS).
cards.note: 100 V pk × 1 A pk = 100 W pk → 50 W avg

cards.front: Preview: what happens to power when V and I are out of phase?
cards.back: During part of each cycle they have opposite signs, so power is negative and flows back to the source. That's reactive power.

cards.front: What is skin effect?
cards.back: With AC, current crowds toward the conductor's surface, which raises its effective resistance.

cards.front: How does skin effect change with frequency?
cards.back: It increases as frequency increases.

cards.front: Does skin effect matter at 60 Hz?
cards.back: For ordinary building wire, no. For large conductors (≈500 kcmil+) and bus bar, yes. That's why NEC Ch. 9 Table 9 lists AC resistance separately.
cards.note: Skin depth in copper at 60 Hz ≈ 8.5 mm

cards.front: How do you reduce skin effect for high-frequency grounding?
cards.back: Use conductors with a lot of surface area: wide copper strap or flat braid.

cards.front: Why do harmonics increase conductor heating?
cards.back: Harmonic currents (180, 300 Hz…) have stronger skin effect and add I²R losses.

cards.front: Why must all conductors of an AC circuit run in the same raceway?
cards.back: A lone conductor heats surrounding steel by induction. Grouping them cancels the field. (NEC 300.3(B), 300.20)
cards.note: Related to, but not the same as, skin effect

cards.front: 240 V AC bridge feeding a crane magnet with 400 V diodes. What must you compare?
cards.back: The diodes' peak rating with the peak of 240 V RMS (≈339 V). Leave margin for high line voltage and spikes.
